blocks.markdown: SSS coverage — objectives: state who is compulsorily covered (Secs. 9, 9-A, 9-B) and who may join voluntarily, apply the employer/employee/employment definitions (Sec. 8(c), (d), (j), (s)), fix effectivity dates (Sec. 10), and trace separation effects (Secs. 11, 11-A) with the Gapayao control-test doctrine.

This lesson tracks syllabus item II.1 in order: when coverage is compulsory (Sec. 9 employees/kasambahay, Sec. 9-A self-employed, Sec. 9-B OFWs), the effect of separation or income interruption (Secs. 11, 11-A), when coverage is voluntary, and when coverage takes effect (Sec. 10). The defined terms in Sec. 8(c), (d), (j), and (s) are the gatekeepers — every coverage question starts by asking whether the worker is an employee, a self-employed person, or neither.

An **employer** is any person running any trade or activity in the Philippines who uses another's services under his orders — except the government and its branches, instrumentalities, and GOCCs. An **employee** is one who renders service for compensation within an employer-employee relationship. A **self-employed** person is both at once, and anyone whose income is not derived from employment falls in the self-employed field.

Read Sec. 8(c) as three elements plus an exclusion: (1) any person, natural or juridical, domestic or foreign; (2) carrying on any trade, business, industry, undertaking, or activity in the Philippines; (3) using another's services under his orders — **except** the government and its political subdivisions, branches, instrumentalities, and GOCCs. Government workers belong to the GSIS, not the SSS. The proviso — a self-employed person is both employee and employer — is the reason self-employed members pay both contribution shares.

Sec. 8(d) defines the employee by relationship, not by job title: service (mental or physical) + compensation + employer-employee relationship. For payroll classification, apply the labor-law **control test** — does the person for whom services are performed have the right to control both the end and the manner and means? Gapayao holds that pakyaw pay, seasonal work, and irregular hours do not defeat employee status where control exists.

Sec. 8(j) carves four exclusions out of 'employment': (1) services with **no employer-employee relationship** (genuine independent contractors are out, but their own crew are covered as the contractor's employees); (2) **Philippine government** service; (3) **foreign government or international-organization** service, unless brought in by agreement with the Philippine Government; (4) services the **Commission excludes by regulation**. Memorize these four — boundary questions (embassy hires, government workers, contractor crews) are decided here.

Sec. 9(a) is the core compulsory rule: **all employees not over 60 — expressly including kasambahays and domestic workers — and their employers**. Private benefit plans integrate rather than substitute: earned benefits cannot be cut, the employer pays SSS first and keeps the balance in the private plan (total cost unchanged), adjustments need agreement, and parties may always top up above the SSS floor. Sec. 9(b) opens the **non-working-spouse** voluntary track for full-time homemakers not otherwise mandatorily covered.

Sec. 9-A makes self-employed coverage **compulsory**, with a non-exclusive enumeration: professionals, partners and single proprietors, listed media workers who are not employees, athletes/coaches/trainers/jockeys, and individual farmers and fishermen. The closing sentence does the heavy lifting — everything applicable to covered employees applies to covered self-employed persons unless the Act says otherwise. A CPA in independent practice and a market vendor are equally, compulsorily covered.

Sec. 9-B — the 2018 rewrite's biggest coverage expansion — makes **all sea-based and land-based OFWs not over 60** compulsorily covered, with the full benefit menu. Sea-based OFWs are employees of their **manning agencies**, which are **solidarily liable** with foreign principals for civil liabilities (controlling persons face criminal liability). Land-based OFWs are treated **as self-employed** (current minimum MSC P8,000) until bilateral agreements shift foreign employers into the employer-share role. Separated OFWs and permanent migrants may continue or join **voluntarily**.

Sec. 10's effectivity triplet: the **employer** from the **first day of operation**, the **employee** from the **day of employment** (no probation or regularization requirement), the **self-employed** upon **registration**. Payroll consequence: withholding starts with the very first payroll period, and the Sec. 24(a) report is due immediately — delay risks damages if a contingency strikes.

Sec. 11: separation ends contribution obligations at the **end of the month of separation**, but paid contributions stay credited and benefit rights survive — there is no forfeiture. The separated employee may keep paying the **total contribution** (both shares) as a voluntary member to preserve full benefit rights. This is the bridge members use to cross the 120/36/3 qualifying thresholds after leaving employment.

Sec. 11-A excuses a self-employed member with **zero income in a month** from paying for that month, with an option to pay voluntarily under the separated-employee rules. The sting is in the proviso: **no retroactive payment** except as Sec. 22-A allows — skipped months stay skipped, depressing the AMSC base and possibly breaking qualifying windows. Seasonal earners must plan voluntary payments forward, never backward.

blocks.markdown: Put it together as a new-hire compliance decision tree. **Step 1 — classify**: employee (control test) → Sec. 9; contractor's crew → contractor's Sec. 9; genuine self-employed → Sec. 9-A; OFW → Sec. 9-B; government hire → GSIS, out of SSS. **Step 2 — clock effectivity**: covered from day one of employment (Sec. 10). **Step 3 — report immediately** (Sec. 24(a)) and **deduct from the first payroll** (Sec. 18). **Step 4 — on separation**: stop at month-end, keep records, and advise the worker on voluntary continuation toward the 120/36/3 thresholds (Sec. 11). Misclassification at Step 1 is the error that creates Sec. 24 damages and Sec. 28 criminal exposure downstream.

**Trap**: 'not over 60' bars NEW compulsory coverage — it does not erase credited contributions or benefit rights already earned. **Trap**: a contractor's workers are not YOUR employees (Sec. 8(j) last sentence), but as principal you are subsidiarily liable for the contractor's SSS civil liabilities and must require a surety bond (Sec. 24(a)). **Trap**: land-based OFWs are treated as self-employed by default — employee-with-foreign-employer treatment needs a bilateral agreement that may not exist.

**Exam memory set**: 60 (age ceiling); operation/employment/registration (effectivity); 4 exclusions of Sec. 8(j); 5 voluntary tracks; control test decides employment (Gapayao); no forfeiture on separation; no retroactive SE payment.

Self-check: (1) A 61-year-old consultant with no employer-employee relationship and no prior SSS record — compulsorily covered? (2) A seafarer hired through a Manila manning agency — who is the employer for SSS purposes? (3) An employee resigns on March 15 — through when do contribution obligations run, and what happens to her 40 posted contributions?

Takeaways: coverage follows the employment relationship (Gapayao's control test); compulsory spans employees/kasambahay, the self-employed, and OFWs, all capped at not over 60; voluntary spans homemakers, continuing members, separated OFWs, and permanent migrants; effectivity runs from operation, employment, or registration; and separation or zero income pauses obligations without forfeiting anything — but skipped SE months can never be backfilled.
